transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Evan (CS), Maya (NovaRetail Head ML), Sam (Platform Eng), Claire (Data Sci)

Summary: Quick review of last week's tuning work, then deep into cost/unit economics - tokens per second per dollar, caching savings, batching experiments and how that changes cost.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep this to 45 mins. quick check - any urgent blockers from last week?
[00:12] Maya: nope just wanted to see the updated numbers on the cost model, we saw Priya's run but need a little more color on what changed when you turned on the prefix cache.
[00:25] Priya: yeah so quick recap, we ran the same test profile with three configs: hosted baseline (gpt-like-32k), quantized variant on dedicated, and dedicated+prefix cache. numbers are rough bc of transcribe but gist is tokens per second improved from ~1,100 to ~1,400 with batching tweaks and to ~1,900 with an effective cache hit of ~45%.
[00:55] Sam: wait that 45% hit-rate, is that on real sessions or synthetic?
[01:02] Priya: it's session-weighted from the replay traces you sent - so closer to production, not synthetic. we saw a lot of reusable prefixes in the support flows which helps a lot.
[01:18] Claire: when you say tokens/sec/$ what exact formula are you using? i want to ensure apples to apples with our internal numbers.
[01:25] Priya: good Q - we're using tokens/sec divided by hourly cost of the instance normalized to dollars; so tokens per second per dollar per hour effectively. Jordan: we put that in the spreadsheet we shared.
[01:40] Jordan: and note that the quantized dedicated run had lower per-token compute but added some variance in tail latency. median was better but p95 got worse by ~30 ms in one run.
[01:55] Maya: p95 is important for us, our customer-facing chat needs tight tail, 200 ms p95 target ideally. do we have numbers on tail w caching?
[02:05] Priya: with prefix cache the p95 improved because we avoided full model passes for cached prefixes, so p95 dropped ~60 ms in those sessions - but only for traffic that benefits, obviously. overall p95 looked like 170-210 ms depending on batch size.
[02:28] Sam: what's the batching profile you used? this is where we get tradeoffs right - tiny batches low latency but low throughput, big batches high throughput cheap but worse latency.
[02:36] Priya: we tried three batch targets: 8, 32, 128. at 8 median token latency was ~80 ms, tokens/sec low; at 32 median ~120 ms, throughput doubled; at 128 median ~210-260 ms. the sweet spot for cost per token was around 32 with cache on.
[02:58] Claire: can you remind me how KV cache works vs prefix cache? I get the name mix up sometimes.
[03:05] Priya: sure - Prefix cache stores entire generated prefixes for identical prompts so we can return cached completions quickly; KV cache stores key-value attention state to speed autoregressive decode when reusing context. in practice they both reduce compute but in different traffic patterns.
[03:20] Jordan: side note, docs sometimes call KV cache K V cash by the auto transcript, haha.
[03:25] Maya: yeah we saw that, lol.
[03:30] Evan: quick commercial note - if you're leaning dedicated because of cost predictability we can lay out reserved capacity pricing vs on-demand in the worksheet. Jordan, can you point to the row with reserved numbers?
[03:40] Jordan: yep - look at the 'reserved_12mo' tab, line items show committed throughput, baseline tokens/sec and unit cost after commitment. with reserved we drop the per-token compute cost by ~18-25% depending on term.
[03:52] Sam: and is that assuming the same quantization level? we tend to prefer 4-bit for perf but worried about quality regressions.
[04:00] Priya: assumption is q4 with selective fp16 fallbacks for layers where quality regressed. in our evals quality delta was negligible for your conversational intents - Claire checked earlier.
[04:12] Claire: yes we ran the 200-sample eval and differences were minor, only edge cases showed hallucination increase, but not for the core flows.
[04:24] Maya: another risk is data residency and audit logs - if we move to dedicated in our VPC we need KMS integration and audit retention 1 year. you have SOC2 docs?
[04:34] Jordan: yes we have SOC 2 Type II and can share the security pack. private/dedicated can be set up with customer-managed KMS and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. we'll schedule a security review next week.
[04:50] Sam: from cost side, can you summarize expected tokens/sec/$ for our baseline traffic? we need a single number to show execs.
[04:58] Priya: rough consolidated number: hosted baseline ~1,100 tps at $0.75/hr equivalent -> ~1,466 tokens/sec/$; dedicated quantized without cache ~1,900 tps/$ equivalent -> ~2,533 tokens/sec/$; with caching those requests that hit cache effectively look like 6-8x cheaper because they bypass decode, so effective tokens/sec/$ for the mix moves to ~3,600 depending on hit-rate.
[05:28] Maya: those are big swings. the cache makes dedicated look much more attractive. but worried about consistency across user cohorts.
[05:36] Priya: totally - that's why we asked for your traffic profile. if support has a lot of reused prompts caching yields outsized benefit; if it's varied search queries, less so.
[05:46] Sam: do you have recommended batch size per route? e.g., chat vs API inference vs embeddings?
[05:52] Priya: yes - chat low-latency route we suggest batch target 8-16 with prefix cache; for async bulk inference or rerank set 64-128. embeddings run much better batched at 512+ on throughput-optimized nodes.
[06:08] Jordan: also routing policy - we can route by policy so sensitive routes use private nodes in your VPC even while lower-sensitivity uses hosted pool. gives hybrid cost wins.
[06:18] Maya: ok that helps. can you walk through the benchmark plan we agreed?
[06:22] Priya: plan: 1) run two 1-hour experiments on your dev replay traces: a) dedicated quantized with cache tuning and batching 32; b) hosted baseline with batching 8. collect metrics: tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, cache hit-rate, cost per 1M tokens. 2) Priya will instrument KV/prefix cache logs, export to CSV. 3) Jordan will compute tokens/sec/$ and update the shared sheet.
[06:44] Claire: for the CSV, can you include request ids and whether the request hit cache, we want to correlate to user segments.
[06:50] Priya: yep we'll include a hashed request id and hit boolean.
[06:55] Sam: any concerns about our seq length distribution affecting the kernel selection? we have a lot of medium-lengths ~1k tokens.
[07:03] Priya: kernel selection adapts but medium-lengths are good for our optimized kernels; long tails might trigger more memory. we'll capture memory pressure metrics in the run.
[07:12] Jordan: can we talk cost sensitivity - what discount threshold makes you choose dedicated?
[07:18] Maya: if committed reserved saves us >20% on expected monthly compute and gives stable latency, that's attractive. also compliance must be met.
[07:26] Jordan: understood. we'll show committed pricing bands and a model showing the break-even.
[07:32] Evan: small note - include cache amortization in the model (engineering time to tune + ops overhead) so it's realistic.
[07:38] Priya: good call, we'll add a line for ops effort and expected hit-rate ramp time.
[07:43] Maya: last question - any limitations we should know about for cold-start traffic spikes?
[07:49] Priya: spikes can be handled with burst capacity on Dedicated or fallback to hosted pool; warm-up latency will be higher for cold LRU misses. recommended warm pools if you expect predictable spikes.
[08:02] Sam: ok great.
[08:05] Jordan: recap and next steps: Jordan send updated cost model by 3/20; Priya run the two 1-hour benchmarks and share CSVs by 3/22; schedule security deep dive for 3/26 - does that work for folks?
[08:18] Maya: yes that's good.
[08:20] Claire: fine with that.
[08:22] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with calendar invites and the worksheet link.

End of call.
